As an avid fan of narrative-driven puzzle games, I recently delved into "The Operator," developed by Bureau 81. Released on July 22, 2024, this game offers a unique experience by placing players in the role of Evan Tanner, an operator at the fictional Federal Defence Intelligence agency. Your primary task is to assist field agents by analysing evidence and providing real-time support, all from behind a computer screen.

The game's immersive design truly makes you feel like a part of a larger investigative team. The puzzles are well-crafted, requiring keen attention to detail without becoming overly frustrating. Each case you handle reveals a piece of a larger conspiracy, keeping your curiosity piqued from start to finish. The narrative is compelling, reminiscent of classic detective stories, and unfolds at a pace that keeps you engaged throughout the approximately five-hour gameplay. 


However, the game isn't without its flaws. Some plot twists are predictable, and the voice acting can be hit-or-miss at times. Additionally, while the main storyline is captivating, I found myself wishing for more side cases to further explore the game's mechanics and world. 


In conclusion, "The Operator" is a commendable addition to the narrative puzzle genre. It offers an immersive and engaging experience that is well worth your time, especially if you're a fan of detective stories and investigative gameplay. Despite its minor shortcomings, it stands out as a solid and enjoyable game.

TLDR: Shorter title but worth the money since it's a good story and it's fun to play the forensics person instead of the usual detective for once. Will be keeping an eye out for future projects from the studio.

Finished in just a bit over two and a half hours, I'd recommend this game to anybody that wants a mystery game where you get to handle the forensic side of things. It's a bit on the shorter side but I'd gladly buy a sequel or a future project from this team if they make one, especially if it's in this style.

 I was expecting the terminal to end up being a bit more relevant after it starts being used but that might be because I was expecting the game to take a sharper turn then it actually did.

Overall the story is pretty good, I was expecting it to take a bit longer to expand the way it did but I'd rather have a 2 - 3 hour game with a good story then a game that drags on for 6 - 8 hours and drops the ball at the end after you've been waiting to see if all of the extra stuff was worth it.

[h1][b] TLDR: Sells itself as an investigative puzzler but delivers a mostly on-rails visual novel experience. The handful of genuine puzzles are great, making their scarcity all the more frustrating.
[/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Neat investigative puzzles (ENHANCE….ENHANCE)
➕Some nice puzzles, like bomb defuse

[h1]NEUTRALS: [/h1]
🔹Story is good, but a bit too on-rails and hand-holding

[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Lots of unskippable intentionally blurry cutscenes leaves a cheap or vague feeling
➖Some reveals are not as big as they should be simply because you wouldn’t know things that your character would know

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world takes place entirely from a computer screen and is set in the 90s, we’re talking older CRT monitor screens. There’s not much exploration to be found, as you work for the government and everything is pretty locked down. I’d say the world is a bit basic and simple, only serving as a UI to show some puzzles. 

The narrative has some good parts. You play as Evan Tanner, a Federal Department of Investigation (FDI) operator, in which your job is to assist field agents. You very quickly learn that there’s something going on and you are enlisted, whether you want to or not, to uncover the truth. 
So while I did enjoy the story to an extent, any scene not at the computer and is told through a characters eyes is a blurry mess of objects that are nearly undecipherable. This could be something related to the story, but I don’t want to give the game the benefit of the doubt here and say that it worsens the experience. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The gameplay seems pretty cool at first, but you quickly realize how on-rails the game is. Essentially, this is a glorified visual novel with a few puzzles sprinkled in. At first, I felt like Garcia from Criminal Minds - I was the internet sleuth assisting agents in the field by giving them on-the-fly information to help with cases. But unfortunately, the game isn’t as cool as that. 
The loop consists of you having a conversation, being presented with evidence, and then using the 2-3 tools at your disposal to answer a question presented by the conversation. For example, you’ll need to identify a killer and a victim by scanning their faces to get their names, then look them up in the FDI database. Same thing with licenses plates or analyzing footage/pictures. It does sound very cool, but I can’t emphasize enough the on-rails experience and lack of deep puzzle mechanics. This is more of a game focused on the narrative. 

The difficulty is forgiving. I’m pretty sure I made every wrong choice in the game, yet still made it to the end. I literally messed up a [spoiler]bomb defuse and got an agent killed[/spoiler]. Whoops. Despite these consequences, this doesn’t seem like it impacted the game as much and wasn’t mentioned again other than a few brief times after the fact. 

[h1] [b] Graphics (Quality/Technical) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Being that the game is from the point of view of a computer screen and all “Real” scenes are a blurry mess, I’d say the quality isn’t great. What footage you do see is grainy 90’s-era quality, but aside from that the computer UI is good and crisp. 

On the technical side, I had no issues, encountered no bugs, and ran the game without issues. 

1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD  

[h1] [b] Audio – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The music isn’t really noticeable, but it does increase in intensity during high-drama parts. 

There is a lot of voice acting, and it all sounds good. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [2/10] [/b] [/h1]
Not a lot of replay value here, unless you want to redo the puzzles again for achievements. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The Operator is described as a game with detective/investigation, and puzzle elements. I’d estimate the game to be about 70% story/narrative focus, 20% puzzles, and 10% deducing or investigating. I’d say that Operator is an okay game, but I was a bit disappointed by the mystery and investigative sides. This is very much a visual novel game more than anything, and as someone that likes visual novels, I was expecting more to use my brain to make deductions instead of clicking pre-defined replies. 

The game does have a few puzzles. I’d say maybe ~10 at the most, and despite that small number, I found them to be good puzzles. Analyzing gunpowder was really cool. Defusing a bomb on the fly was also great. If the game was more focused on gameplay like that, then I’d give it a much higher score, but these are the highest highs that The Operator offers, and there’s only a few of them. 

The real focus of the game is on the narrative. While I wouldn’t consider the narrative to be bad, there were a few parts that were either ridiculously obvious, or a missed opportunity. 
Obvious, because of metagaming - anyone who watches mystery shows knows that there’s only so many characters who could be the culprit due to you the show introducing them to the viewer. Same concept here, it’s obviously going to be the handful of people you know about already. 
Missed opportunity because you as the player only know what you know. One part in particular [spoiler]has the player finding out his apartment is being watched with a camera, and you have to identify whose apartment it is[/spoiler]. Well how can you possibly figure that out without knowing anything about the characters' life, nor ever having been there? Dumb. 

Overall, I do recommend The Operator, but it’s important that you know what you’re going into. This is NOT about deduction or investigating, and that’s not necessarily a bad thing, but I feel the game presents itself in a way that it’s something that it isn’t. 

[h1] [b] Recommend? (Price) [Y/N] [/b] [/h1]
[h1]Yes[/h1]
$14 base price is a bit much for a ~5 hour game with very low replay value. Wait for a sale. Around ~$5-7 would be a good point.

review_text_raw:
The Operator, developed by Bureau 81 and published by Bureau 81 together with indienova, is a tightly focused narrative puzzle game that transforms the quiet, procedural work of intelligence analysis into a tense and engaging thriller. Rather than placing players in the role of an action hero or field agent, the game casts them as a desk-bound operator, someone whose power comes not from physical presence but from information, observation, and deduction. This shift in perspective defines the entire experience, creating a game that feels intimate, cerebral, and deliberately restrained.

You play as Evan Tanner, a newly recruited operator working for the fictional Federal Department of Intelligence. Your job is to support agents in the field by analysing data, processing evidence, and drawing connections that others might miss. The game unfolds almost entirely through Evan’s workstation, presented as a simulated computer desktop filled with databases, analysis tools, messaging systems, and case files. This interface-driven approach immediately sets the tone: instead of cinematic spectacle, The Operator relies on immersion through routine, making the player feel like they are genuinely sitting at a government terminal late at night, piecing together fragments of truth.

Gameplay revolves around solving a series of cases that gradually escalate in complexity and importance. Early tasks feel procedural—identifying suspects, tracing movements, or cross-referencing records—but as the story unfolds, patterns begin to emerge and the stakes rise. Players are required to closely read documents, examine photos and videos, search databases, and interpret subtle clues hidden in plain sight. The puzzles reward attentiveness and logical reasoning, often asking players to synthesize information from multiple sources rather than relying on a single obvious answer. When a breakthrough occurs, it feels earned, the result of careful thought rather than trial and error.

As the narrative progresses, the game shifts from isolated casework into a broader conspiracy. A mysterious hacker begins to interfere with FDI systems, raising questions about surveillance, authority, and the reliability of the information you’re working with. This transition adds narrative tension without abandoning the game’s grounded tone. The story remains largely linear, but it is effectively paced, allowing suspense to build gradually as seemingly unrelated assignments reveal deeper connections. Dialogue and character interactions are understated, delivered through calls, messages, and system prompts rather than dramatic cutscenes, which reinforces the feeling that you are always working behind the scenes.

One of the game’s greatest strengths is how convincingly it uses its interface as both a storytelling and gameplay tool. Every window, search bar, and analysis program feels purposeful, and learning how to use these tools becomes part of the experience. While some mechanics are simplified or exaggerated for gameplay purposes, they remain believable within the fiction, maintaining immersion. The design encourages players to slow down, double-check assumptions, and think critically—mistakes often stem from overlooking details rather than misunderstanding mechanics.

Visually, The Operator embraces a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic inspired by older operating systems and institutional software. The interface is dense but readable, intentionally lacking visual flair in favor of authenticity. This design choice may feel dry to some players, but it suits the game’s themes perfectly, emphasizing bureaucracy, control, and the monotony of surveillance work. Subtle audio cues, ambient hums, and restrained music enhance tension without distracting from concentration, allowing the player’s focus to remain on the task at hand.

In terms of pacing, the game strikes a careful balance. It is compact, typically completed in a handful of hours, but it avoids feeling rushed. Each case builds naturally on the last, and the increasing narrative weight keeps momentum strong. The linear structure limits replayability, as choices rarely branch into significantly different outcomes, but this also allows the developers to maintain tight narrative control and deliver a coherent, focused story without filler.

Community reception reflects appreciation for the game’s originality and execution. Players who enjoy detective work, mystery narratives, and “games on a computer” style experiences frequently praise its atmosphere and puzzle design. Criticism tends to focus on its short length, limited player agency, and occasional moments where immersion is broken by game-like constraints. Even so, these issues rarely overshadow the strengths of the experience, particularly for players aligned with its intended audience.

Taken as a whole, The Operator is a confident and distinctive narrative puzzle game that finds tension in observation rather than action. It succeeds by committing fully to its premise, turning data analysis and desk work into compelling gameplay through thoughtful design and strong thematic focus. While it may not appeal to players seeking open-ended systems or high replay value, it offers a memorable, tightly constructed experience for those who enjoy slow-burn storytelling, logical deduction, and the quiet unease of uncovering truths from behind a screen.

Rating: 9/10

I have to say I was absolutely hooked with the concept of [i] The Operator. [/i] One watch of the trailer will tell you why; an operator helping with government investigations, analyzing clues, basically being the man-in-the-chair? It's all awesome! But what killed the mood for me was the cliche writing, amateur voice acting, and the simplistic puzzles. First of all the writing. Who TALKS like this?! Every person you meet is quippy, chippy, or clever with their line delivery. These don't sound like professional field agents, they sound like cartoon characters. A man has been killed, TAKE THIS SERIOUSLY! They should be more realistic, a bit grittier, more direct. And why am I doing everything? What exactly is your job here??

Next are the puzzles. They are already simple enough, but I feel babied and talked down to by the characters we meet. The game would make itself so much more compelling if there were harder applications! Something I had to grill through to find what my agent needed. So far, I can click two buttons and get the answer to the riddle. I don't [i] feel [/i] like a secret agent, which is what I bought the game for. And not to mention the game's animations for security footage, which are taken so seriously for how poor in quality they are. The tone simply doesn't match. 

Finally, I had a sincerely hard time caring about the story of the game. The plot was mildly interesting, conspiracies and hackers and whatnot, but it didn't land. Mainly because it meant wading through monologues from the characters, which drove me insane. If the game was harder, there would be much more to invest in. I would feel accomplished! But after completing the first two days, I feel like there was no other option but to succeed. There was never any risk of me failing, which made it hard for me to connect to the game at all. In the end it was not the experience I was expecting, and if you're looking to be a tech-savvy sleuth, look elsewhere.

EDIT: I've been thinking about this a lot, and I just wanted to add one more thing. You can see how I go into quite a bit of initial, just-coming-down-off-finishing-the-game detail down below if you'd like, but I'd like to quickly say here, at the start, that I think a big part of the issue was a fundamental misunderstanding of what this game was. I went into this expecting a puzzle game, but it isn't so much a puzzle game as it is a story game.
I feel it's advertised as more of a puzzle game with subtle hints at an overarching story you might be able to uncover, and indeed it does *play* like a puzzle game... until it very much becomes about following the narrative.
My feelings below still stand - including the ones after my spoiler tags - but while I don't know that I would've felt *differently* if I'd gone into this expecting something different, much of my confusion and disappointment might've been at least softened.

ORIGINAL REVIEW:
Overall, I was pretty disappointed with this game.
First, it was incredibly short - I had the game open for 7-ish hours... but I had dinner, fed the dogs, took a shower, yada yada, with it paused, so I'm not actually sure how long it really took. Most of the puzzles themselves weren't particularly challenging - though the mechanics were satisfying in a point-and-click, ASMR kind of way - and then one or two of the puzzles were SUPER, out-of-pocket complicated, insanely difficult, and totally out of place?? And because of the length of the game, I felt like all the mechanics I was learning, I really didn't need for very long, or often even more than once.
The writing, acting, sound design, and off-screen auditory storytelling were beautiful. Very well done; you can tell a lot of love went into it, there just... wasn't a whole lot of content.

I saw someone mention that if there were an "operator mode," that would make up for a lot of this problem, and I agree. *MILD SPOILER* Every single one of the cases were directly linked to the main story, and I think being able to enjoy some of the mechanics for longer would make it feel a little more worthwhile. Again, many of the puzzles were fairly simple, but it was still fun and satisfying in a way, and then it would also be more impactful - learning how to do the more complicated puzzles - because you'd have to use that knowledge again.

**SPOILERS FOR THE END**

The ending was incredibly dissatisfying to me. I immediately got off and looked to see if I somehow got "the bad ending" and there was another way I could've played to get "the good ending," but no. It is what it is - one and done. review_text_raw:
My recommendation is heavily conditional. If you are into conspiracies and point-and-click games with simple puzzle elements, I would recommend this at around $10. If you don't fall into those categories, then you aren't the target demographic and I can't recommend it. Overall Operator is not a bad game - in fact, I would really like to see more content for this, or perhaps even more games like it - but it's held back by a few flaws.

First, The Good:
[list]
    [*]The setting and overall theme is great. You play as a deskbound investigator at the not-FBI, using your computer to sift through clues and work with field agents to investigate crimes. Naturally, this leads to uncovering conspiracies and shadowy organizations.
    [*]The gameplay is intuitive and accessible. You will never have to pixel-hunt for your clues; when you're inspecting a piece of evidence, the things that your gut tell you are important to the case usually are, and they're usually clickable.
    [*]The story is fun, interesting, and will keep you engaged. It references some real-world "conspiracies" that actually happened.
    [*]The gameplay loop feels fresh. I know games in this format have been done before, but it's been a while since I've seen it executed like this. I don't know of many recent games that are quite like it.
[/list]

Next, The Bad:
[list]
    [*]The puzzles are a bit simple. At times it feels like more of a visual novel than a detective/investigation game.
    [*]Many of the plot twists are predictable. The dramatic reveals towards the end of the game didn't land with me at all because I had already seen them coming way ahead of time.
    [*]Sometimes there are clues that fall into your lap a little too easily, to the point where it doesn't feel believable. The most egregious example: [spoiler]During one investigation, you find the buried body of a scientist who worked on a secret government project. The people involved with the project had him killed to keep him quiet. For some reason, they buried him in a marked grave, near the marked graves of a hundred of the project's victims, wearing his full lab coat, with his work ID showing full name and place of employment still in a cord around his neck, and with unwiped floppy disks in his pocket that contained all of his research and notes.[/spoiler]
    [*]The game is filled with anachronisms. It's supposed to be set in 1992, but it doesn't even attempt to maintain this setting. Everybody has a cell phone, which in the 90s were expensive, rare, and had very limited coverage; the computer used by main character appears to have a multi-core CPU, which didn't exist until the 2000s; and one of the early investigations involves a digital camera with a large preview screen, which also did not exist in 1992. All of this is like having a character use an iPhone in a video game about Operation Desert Storm; it can be immersion-breaking. Operator probably should have been set in the mid- to late-2000s, not 1992.
    [*]At the time of writing, there is only one ending, and it feels rushed. [spoiler]Outside of one minor detail regarding a side character, your choices don't matter.[/spoiler]
    [*]The last and most obvious drawback is probably the one you've seen mentioned in other reviews: this is a short game. It'll probably only take you around 3 hours to complete. The cynic in me wonders if this was done intentionally to get around the 2-hour Steam refund limit.
[/list]

I did enjoy my time with Operator; if you're like me, and enjoy the thought of playing detective and uncovering government conspiracies, you probably will too. Ultimately I think this is a decent game with a solid concept behind it, but the problems I listed above hold me back from recommending this unconditionally. In particular, I feel that Operator is slightly overpriced when measured against the amount of gameplay time you're likely to get out of it. This seems to be the developer's first game, so I'm hoping that they take the lessons learned from Operator and continue to improve on this formula.

review_text_raw:
The Operator offers a remarkably engaging narrative experience, supported by a strong storyline and a well-executed plot twist. The structure of each case is thoughtfully designed: from the call system to the investigative tasks, every step feels purposeful and polished. Working through evidence, analyzing data, and piecing together conclusions is consistently satisfying and stands out as one of the game’s greatest strengths.

Because the investigative tools and the workstation interface are so enjoyable to use, I found myself wishing for a mode that would provide long-term engagement beyond the main story. The campaign can be completed relatively quickly, and once it ends, the gameplay loop—despite being excellent—comes to an abrupt stop.

A dedicated free-play or “ongoing operations” mode could meaningfully extend the game’s lifespan. For example, players could receive procedurally generated cases or scenario-based assignments that scale in complexity, allowing them to continue applying the tools and systems introduced in the main storyline. This would give players who enjoy the investigative process a space to keep refining their skills and exploring the mechanics without a fixed ending.

I am very much looking forward to The Operator 2, and I genuinely believe that adding an optional long-term mode—whether free-play, case generator, or rotating scenario board—would significantly enhance replay value and increase the game’s overall appeal.

For anyone considering this title: the core experience is absolutely worth it, and the investigative gameplay is exceptionally well-crafted. The story alone justifies the €14 price, and I can recommend it without hesitation.

review_text_raw:
While a very polished and well-crafted experience, this game has a number of fatal flaws that undermine and eventually irrevocably cripple your enjoyment of it.  Firstly, it's incredibly short.  I do understand that this tends to be the case for these kinds of games, crafting content for them is much more effort intensive than it is for other genres, but even by the standards of other games in this genre, you get very little playtime compared to its cost.  This is further exacerbated by a complete lack of replay value, as the story is completely linear and has no alternate endings, though there are a few pieces of content not central to the story that the player can find through their own initiative.  If you take nothing else from this review and do decide to buy the game, buy it on sale, the existing content doesn't really justify the price point.

To get into the real reasons this is a negative review, as money alone wouldn't have been enough to get me to write this, we need to first revisit the game's linearity.  The game does provide the illusion of choice, but none of the choices the player can make matter, and acting as though they do will inevitably see the game yanking on your leash and railroading you back to the single story it wants to tell.  This linearity continues to the mysteries that form the game's content, as they are designed so that the player is forced to solve them linearly as well.  Rather than providing multiple angles of attack, players must solve one specific part of a mystery before progressing to the next one, so for the most part you don't get that feeling of everything coming together as multiple clues and leads snap together into a single image, though there are exceptions to this.  I can't get too much into the ending without spoiling players, but it was abrupt, unsatisfying, and served to terminate any remaining sense of agency I had.  Everything I had accomplished was undone in an instant, in a way that felt, frankly, disrespectful and contemptuous to me as a player.  The entire point of a game, the thing that fully differentiates it from other forms of media, is that the person consuming it has agency, is not simply a passive observer but actively engages with and shapes the piece of media that they are consuming.  Of all the games I've played, this embraces that principle the least, and suffers for it.

The ultimate sin of The Operator, however, the one no detective game can be forgiven for, is its predictability.  I am in no way talented when it comes to mysteries.  When I play a detective game, read a mystery novel, or watch a movie in those genres, I am generally unable to put together the pieces ahead of time and figure out the twist before it is presented to me.  This was not the case with The Operator.  I was able to determine most of the major narrative twists well ahead of time, because they were fairly obviously telegraphed.  There were a few that were well done, and there were some that would have been very good if other obvious elements hadn't telegraphed them ahead of time.  Anyone playing this game will likely figure out its main narrative twists well before they are presented to the player, and that is truly tragic.

The Operator – 8/10 – A Tense and Captivating Dive into Espionage

The Operator is a stealth-driven, psychological thriller that plunges players into the shadowy world of covert operations, high-stakes intelligence, and moral ambiguity. With an engaging narrative and a compelling atmosphere, it combines tactical gameplay with deep narrative exploration, offering a gripping experience for fans of espionage games. While it may not reinvent the wheel, The Operator does a great job of delivering a tightly-paced, immersive story that keeps you on the edge of your seat.

In The Operator, you play as a field agent working for a secretive government agency, tasked with handling covert missions that blur the lines between right and wrong. The game is heavy on stealth and strategy, as you navigate through a series of complex scenarios—whether infiltrating a heavily guarded facility, gathering intelligence, or neutralizing a threat. The gameplay is tense and slow-paced, with an emphasis on thinking ahead, blending in with your surroundings, and making choices that can lead to either success or failure. It’s all about staying unseen, listening for clues, and using your limited resources wisely. The tension constantly builds as you wonder if you’ll be caught or if the consequences of your decisions will haunt you later on.

The game’s mechanics are simple but effective. You don’t have a full arsenal at your disposal like in many action-heavy titles, and that’s part of the charm. The focus here is on patience, strategy, and managing the few tools you have, whether it’s a silenced pistol or hacking equipment. The difficulty comes not from constant firefights but from the challenge of navigating through dangerous environments, avoiding detection, and managing the relationships and choices you make along the way.

One of The Operator’s strongest points is its atmosphere. The game does an excellent job of crafting a sense of isolation and tension, using sound design, lighting, and environment to its advantage. The dark, minimalist environments add to the oppressive mood, and the voice acting and soundtrack complement the sense of secrecy and paranoia that runs throughout the game. You always feel like you’re being watched, and every decision could push you deeper into the world of shadowy operatives and untrustworthy allies.

The narrative is intriguing and filled with twists, as you’ll often have to decide whether to follow orders or act according to your own moral compass. The story doesn’t just follow the usual espionage tropes—it explores themes of trust, betrayal, and the emotional toll of being part of a covert operation. The characters you meet, especially the ones you interact with the most, are well-written and add layers of complexity to the plot. The game gives you enough room to shape your own interpretation of events, but it doesn’t shy away from showing the darker consequences of a life lived in secrecy.

However, The Operator does have its shortcomings. The stealth mechanics, while solid, can feel repetitive at times, especially in the later levels where the pacing slows down significantly. There are also a few technical hiccups, like occasional AI pathfinding issues or moments when the game’s visuals don’t quite match the level of detail of the environments. Some players may also find the slower pace a bit tedious, particularly if they’re expecting a more action-packed experience.

8/10 – A Solid, Tense Espionage Experience
The Operator is a highly effective stealth game that delivers a tense, engaging experience for anyone who loves espionage narratives. While its mechanics might feel repetitive in certain sections, the atmosphere, story, and the moral complexity of the choices you make keep it captivating throughout. The game’s slow pace and emphasis on stealth give it a unique edge in a genre often dominated by faster-paced action. If you’re a fan of games that require patience and strategic thinking, The Operator will keep you hooked. It might not be perfect, but it’s a well-executed, atmospheric title that leaves a lasting impression.

review_text_raw:
This review is unfortunate, because as much as I'd like to recommend the game, there's a few gripes I have with it.

First and foremost, I want to stress, this game is great and has a good hook for its plot. The mechanics it employs are varied and fun, and you do get to feel like an FBI agent working on cases alongside others. The game does a lot to nail the feel and vibe, the UI is also great and intuitive. The game's main issue isn't one singular thing, rather, it's a collection of small, minor nitpicks that ultimately end up souring the entire experience. Without trying to spoil anything, I'm going to try and summarise my complaints. 

First and foremost, the ending left me wanting. If there was an alternate ending you could achieve by using information you've gathered, it'd be one thing, but you don't get to do anything and then it just sort of ends abruptly, teasing a sequel or DLC. This is the very definition of a cliffhanger, and as such, extremely unsatisfying.

This could have been remedied if the game length was longer. But the game's barely clocking in 3 hours, you could probably beat it in 2. And, likely because of said short runtime, the game features a very small cast of characters. This unfortunately results in a somewhat predictable list of potential suspects, lessening any impacts felt from reveals that you likely saw coming.

Perhaps my biggest disappointment with how short the game was, is that the actual mechanics were unique and interesting! The puzzles were good and it introduced so many systems, one time you're analyzing chemical compounds based on formulas, another time you're disarming a bomb while given a huge manual of possibilities. And each of these varied activities happens exactly once. You spend all that time learning, understanding and mastering a skill only for it to literally not be relevant again.

This all could have perhaps been remedied by a sort of "endless mode" that generates cases and solutions, but that does not exist. And likely never will, because the game is far more focused on "immersion" as a central mechanic than gameplay. You spend a good solid 20 minutes of said 3 hours being forced to watch "immersive" unskippable cutscenes that did not need to last as long as they did. I say "immersive", because they use minimalism and only show you blurry, obfuscated imagery, which is kind of neat and saves on budget, but also means you don't even get eye candy.

Ultimately, this feels like a passion project with the wrong focus, which is a shame, because what it does right, it excels at. It's difficult to recommend this when there's games such as Cyber Manhunt 1 & 2 out that cost less and are far, far more superior in terms of value and vision. The devs are talented, and I will keep a close eye on any of their future projects, but if "The Operator 2" doesn't provide something substantially more... substantial, I can't see myself recommending that either.

review_text_raw:
Conspiratorial thinking is kinda like anime girls. Like, okay. So there's this super hot princess from planet catgirl who's on the run from the space mafia, and she just so happens to teleport naked right into your bathtub. While you're in it. And because of this, she's super into you for some reason. Yeah, sounds nice, but this is so insanely removed from how actual relationships form, it's like watching aliens mate (I mean... she is an alien, so...)

And with conspiracies it's like: okay, so there's this ultra-powerful cabal of politicians, billionaires and celebrities, who completely control the society without being spotted... but then they reveal themselves by using symbols in plain sight. And the person to stop them? A bumbling born-into-wealth TV-star who in fact is a 5D-chess player, so all his obvious mistakes are actually genius moves that you just don't get. I don't know guys, seems very legit, but there are a few pieces of this story that make me question its validity.

Think about how a real conspiracy of this scale would work. Incomprehensible wealth would be poured into world-class assassins and operatives to ensure compliance or silence. Evidence would be erased with brutal efficiency, with red herrings and multiple layers of scapegoats; but even then, people are people, and eventually something could possibly slip the cracks. 

The Operator explores this more realistic portrayal of conspiracies, with the scale also being somewhat more realistic. You don't know who you can trust and who you can't. But not everyone (except you) is in on it.

Right?

But hold on. Before you start yelling LOOMINARTY CONFIRMED and smoking dat 420 MLG style, some actual work needs to be done. You're an [strike]FBI[/strike] FDI operator with an access to a pretty sweet database, but also a job to do - to support agents in the field. Whatever confirming of loominarty you'll be doing will have to be squeezed in between protecting and serving those who [strike]are supposed to[/strike] protect and serve. Or perhaps these things could be related?

Wouldn't that be convenient.

Even with all your state-of-the-art tech you'll still have to think outside the box here. And pay attention. You might not find the all-seeing eye, but a funny detail here, a reappearing pattern there, and you just might find something that you're not supposed to.

But it's a dangerous game. For you, and for whoever [i]they[/i] might see as your ally. Things might get tense. Your palms will sweat, your heart will go a little bit faster. Someone's life might be on the line. And you're the only one that picked up the phone.

Still: this little journey might have what you could call flaws. I won't tell you what they are, because I think they don't really alter the value of the experience. You're a clever person; I'm sure you can see what I mean.

(if you're not that clever, you might want to skip this one, I've seen some really funny comments on the forums from people getting stuck because they missed some stuff)

And if my words alone don't convince you, you might want to know that the (achievement-sourced) percentage of people who have beaten the game is 67%. The only game with a number higher than this is Linelith, but that's a puzzle game that can be beaten in an hour. Draw your own conclusions.

This game has so much going on that I would ideally like to praise but a lot of those same things are also why I didn't really enjoy it.  On the bright side it has a very clever user interface system I like where most of the game is controlled via a "computer", the puzzles range from really easy to more complicated, and the story has some creativity going on.  It's definitely somewhat interesting, very dialogue heavy, and I would not recommend if you're not a strong reader, lover of puzzle games, or if you like a lot of scenery or environment changes.

With that said, the user interface becomes tiring to interact with very quickly.  It's hard to convey a sense of importance or immediate action when most of the puzzles really come down to clicking and having a computer "analyze" random clues.  The puzzles don't scale well in difficulty nor do they feel like they have a good payoff - any skill you learn will either be used again and again because we have to have some way to drive the game or it's a one time use - why did we bother to spend so much time reworking the wheel for no reason? (Example slight spoiler: you will never need to analyze anything other than the one sample in the game).  The instructions are lacking a lot - they have a help button that is definitely useful but there's an element of figure it out here that at times seems un-necessary.  I really don't understand not sticking to more tried and true puzzle formats particularly because they would have felt more rewarding, helped the game, and surely been easier to execute with more precision.

The story is the last complaint I'm going to throw out there.  It's interesting and I want to be invested, however, it is rushed, let down by a lot of bad music and sound interaction, and I found myself uninvested in the characters including my own character frequently.  Any story is going to ask you to slightly engage in disbelief but if you're an analytical or practical thinker there is going to come a point where you realize this is almost like a bad tv fiction.  If you're ever watched a non believable show you enjoyed - something like bones comes to mind - this is taking the worse parts of we can rush a story, analysis, evidence, data, blah blah blah but without any of the charm of why it matters.

Interesting idea but a bit of a miss on execution for me and kind of a feeling of  . . .  why did I spend time on this? lol.

[h1] Short and fun little deep state conspiracy game [/h1] 

First of all, this game is short.[b] VERY SHORT [/b]. It takes about 3-4 hours to complete, but the game tells the story it wants to tell in that time so it´s fine. 

[h3] Story 7/10 [/h3] 
The story is fine. It starts of strong, leaving you as the operator to figure out what you are doing and why you are doing it.
As soon as the story picks up the pace, the game is beginning to get more and more predictable. Sure, it makes sure to tell the story in a convincing way, but if the player has had any contact with books that follow similar plotlines or watched a few "rogue agent fighting conspiracy" movies you know where the plot is going and how the game will end. Ending was fine, a bit disappointing because the cut was fast and hard and resulted in a cliff hanger. To me it feels like the devs wrote a story thats about 10 hours long and just cut the game in half when they had the opportunity to do so, preparing the player for a future sequel.

[b] STORY SPOILERS [/b]
[spoiler] In my opinion the reveal that Mike Trench, our friend and FDI director, is the mole and head of the "Operator Program" was very predictable about half-way through  the game (ever since the Biolab incident and the player operator talking about "baiting out the mole"). The Ghost was written in a very stereotypical bad guy hitman way: I dont have a name, my identity was erased. I know the truth but can not tell you. You can ask any question as long as it is not "out of bounds". Yeah, very corny and kinda cringy. In general, even though the way it is written is good and convincing for the most part, sometimes the game feels like the devs wanted to take the easy way out in a few situations (Player being Sasha Cole, Xavier actually being a friend of HAL, the Ghost just escaping like nothing happened and being able to interfere with HALs scripts...) But hey, for what it is, it´s a solid experience. [/spoiler] 

[h3] Music 7/10 [/h3] 
Pretty good, especially the main menu music. But not memorable. Just nice BGM. Not really worth paying for the OST imo but who am i to decide.

For me the games strong points are the art direction or visual direction in combination with the player interacting with the desktop. It really immerses you in your role as the operator and you really feel like you are investigating CCTV footage and sifting through documents to find small clues. The game really takes you out of this illusion by having to click the objective and then clicking the requested information. Not a fan of that, could have been integrated in a more smooth and immersive way. Audio design is great too, the voice acting feels believable enough and the sound effects are accurate and synced well. Nothing really to complain about there.

Overall it is a fun, short and interesting game with a few flaws that can be overlooked. Wait for a sale before you buy it though, for 3-4 hours of playtime it is just a bit too much (About 1€/$ per hour of playtime should be standard imo).

The game really was not what I expected. From the store page, I thought it would be fairly puzzle focused, with a lot of scanning evidence and connecting dots. But in reality, it plays out more like a visual novel with some very simple puzzles thrown in. There were multiple elements that seemed like they would be recurring features, but were used a single time and never again. Many pieces of evidence are teased, but are never actually shown before the game ends. The game feels like it ends *way* too quickly. It took me just over three hours to finish. I'm fine with shorter games, but there's so much potential here that goes nowhere because the game ends so soon.

On the plus side, the presentation is great. Despite mostly being a computer screen, the visuals have a certain flare to them that leans into the setting. The soundtrack compliments the narrative at every step, swelling at big reveals and calming down after tense moments. And the voice actors give solid performances. No complaints on this aspect.

As for the narrative, it's fairly compelling. You can definitely see a lot of the twists coming before they happen, but the presentation makes it interesting to see play out regardless. That being said, it again suffers from being too short. You're meant to be unraveling a big conspiracy over the course of the game, but by the time it's over, it feels like you've barely stuck your toes in. I was invested in what was happening, had just had a big reveal, and then... suddenly the credits are rolling.

There are definitely things to like about this game, but I have a hard time recommending it, especially if your mostly here for that "Investigation" tag. It's too short, too easy, and doesn't quite live up to what it says on the box. It feels like a demo for a larger game, but I kind of just wanted the larger game to begin with.

review_text_raw:
Yet another case where a "neutral" review option would be a great feature on steam.

The Operator is somewhat summed up as an detective esk simulator game where the bulk of the gamelay loop is behind your desk, gathering evidence & solving cases by connecting the dots. It was clearly inspired by games such as Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You, Song of Farca and the likes, so if that's up your alley you'll most likely also enjoy this one.

Though: an unfortunate difference between those games and this one is both the depth & usage of the built in systems/tools at your disposal, the very linear story, and the playtime of the game. Starting with the latter, a normal playthrough of the game sits around 2 to 3 hours. As the game is very linear in terms of choices you can make (the choices only change a few minor responses, there is only a singular ending and your choices don't affect this) there is not really a great reason to replay the game unless you're going for all achievements; as some are missable on a first playthrough.

Which makes the price, +-14EUR (without sale, as of writing this), a complicated point.

Apart from the playtime, the game makes up for it by the amazing voice acting (not AI generated), _amazing_ polished look and feel (you can clearly see a lot of love and thought were poured into this) and really interesting scenes (artistic direction wise) splattered between days. All in all, really good experience and amazing opener; especially for an indie developer. (there are some minor complaints such as the chat stealing your focus when having to make a choice preventing you from typing in a different window, but nothing game breaking.) -- Just in the end wished with this much work & love put into it, the story was a tad longer.

My final gripe was the somewhat limited use and complexity of the tools given to you. It goes hand in hand with the point about playtime, because how else would you utilize a lab analysis tool or terminal if not by expanding the story. There were tools that looked really interesting, but are in the end just used once; which is a shame really. The times you do utilize them are fun and all feel unique.

So. All in all, a really solid game that I see more so as a foundation for something bigger. It at times feels more like a demo than an full game story wise. If you don't mind the price for what you're getting, and games like orwell are up your alley; you'll enjoy this one. But it may be better to wait for the operator 2 (which is currently in development!) or play a similar game if you're looking for a longer story or if you don't prefer the linear story style of this game.


In the end I'd give it a 6.5/10. Absolutely loved what it had, but left me wanting more. Wunderforce described it perfectly in another review: "Clearly the quality is top-notch but it's a bit baffling someone would put so much work into something so short. This makes it almost feel like a long demo."

review_text_raw:
My experience with The Operator can be summed up as follows: great presentation, limited investigation.  It's a  game that looks sharp, feels polished, and tells a story that is rather entertaining, yet never quite trusts you enough to truly investigate it on your own. I enjoyed my time with it. I just kept wishing it would let me off the leash.

The production is slick from top to bottom. The performances sell the drama, and the narrative momentum keeps you moving even when a few plot holes start to peek through if you linger too long on the details. It is a fun story. It just is not a particularly demanding one.

Let’s be clear about something. This is not really an investigation game.

You are deliberately guided from one beat to the next with little room to wander or hope oiff the beaten path. That keeps the pacing tight, sure, but it also strips away the thrill of deduction that hallmarks great detective games . No alternate paths, no clever lateral thinking moments, no opportunities to feel like you outsmarted the system. Outside of one genuinely challenging, spoiler free sequence that actually made me pause and think, most of the puzzles feel straightforward and simple to resolve.

And then there is the ending. I assumed I had stumbled into the Bad Ending because of something I had done wrong, only to realize that this was simply... the finish. And I figured it was disappointing.

This game didn't scratch my detective game itch. I love having my detective instincts tested. I enjoy piecing together clues and trusting my logic to guide me. I wanted more depth, more resistance. That said, for someone easing into detective style games for the first time, this is an excellent starting point. As long as you're picking it up on sale.

TL;DR: This game is a 3-hour long visual novel with not-that-meaningful choices, good music and sound effects, narration, and an interesting but short linear story line. 0 replay-ability.

The nice things:

[spoiler]1. The cutscenes where the game shows you that time has passed is nice. The subtle drug-taking noises and coughing noises makes a good addition. Even though there is no real graphics here, it shows that the developers put in a lot of efforts in making the game immersive.
2. The interface and UI, especially the keyboard noises you make when you are typing, makes me reminiscent of a time when I wasn't even alive. It just feels nice to type things and click on things.
3. Narration is good, not crazy impressive, but good. That's a hard bar to pass by my standards.
4. Mechanics are nice, problem solving feels rewarding, visual and audio clues are subtle yet noticeable.[/spoiler]

The first playthrough of the game is amazing, but there are a few nick-picking things.

[spoiler]1. Agents not reacting differently when you call them by their first names instead of their last names.
2. During the first interaction with HAL, I chose to report her to my supervisor. And after the second one, I ratted her out again because I felt even if she helped me she is still wanted for good reasons. Even when I ratted her out twice, she still choose to help me with mellow tones and such. I'd expect some type of pissed-off-but-still-have-to-work-with-you type of attitude. (This can be explained with later plots but, a pissed-off reaction would've been nice, it would feel like the game recognized my choices.)
3. During the agent Andrews infiltration event, the security camera added immersion but served little to no purpose. She could complete her task no matter what, and even though we spotted for her to avoid the walking personnel, it didn't seem to matter because the guy didn't do anything when he literally saw her in the first pass.
4. I just finished my second playthrough, this game has 0 replay-ability. Everything is the same, your choices don't matter where the story goes, Tanner will always die in the end. I guess its building for a potential sequal.
5. The game teased the true identity of the Mike waaaaaay too easy. As the head of the entire secret service unit, you would go ahead and call 'your friend' during work through secured line just chatting? Also, he lied about having a wife while his files show that he is single. Meanwhile the game constantly push how weird Skinner is but they exposed the lead on Mike way too early and way too easily.[/spoiler]

Finally, if you have finished the game.
[spoiler]Can anyone tell me what 25000100193555 means? This code is written in the ALICE file in your trashbin if you open the folder before HAL gives you the code. If you open it again after HAL gives you the code it updates to the usual letter from Alice. The code doesn't open any files in the HDD, I wonder what its used for, its the only remaining mystery in this game for me.[/spoiler]

review_text_raw: I can't in good conscience give this game a good review, but I also can't give it a poor review. It's times like this I wish Steam had a middle-ground review option. This game was very fun and scratched an itch I didn't know I had. However, labeling it as an investigation game or describing it the way it does is misleading. Yes, there is some investigation, but there's really only one singular crime to solve. The storyline is very linear and easy to guess. If it were marketed as a game about solving a singular crime, that would be accurate, but it misleads you in the description by stating, 'Investigate mysterious crimes. Use cutting-edge FDI software to dig for clues, solve puzzles, and uncover the truth.' This is incorrect. You only use most of the 'software' exactly once, after implying you should read the extensive manual that comes along with it. This is a game that you could probably finish within 2-3 hours, which also doesn't justify its price. Honestly, they could have dropped the mid-tier storyline and just made a game along the lines of Criminal Minds or CSI, where you use these tools to try to solve cases, and it would be infinitely more fun. I know I'm probably the outlier here with my review, and I will say I did enjoy what they had, but it just wasn't what they promised in their wording and descriptions (maybe I misunderstood some stuff, who knows). There does seem to be an open door for expansions in the future, but if they're along the same timeframe as this game and offer only 2-3 hours of playtime, they should drastically reduce the price because as it stands, it felt like an expensive tech demo.

Very nice game but very short with no replayability so highly recommended, but I'd suggest on discounted price.

review_text_raw:
I wanted to love this game but I just cannot recommend you spend money on what is ultimately a disappointing experience. 

The game has a great concept with a strong atmosphere, and what I hoped was great potential but the overall experience ends up feeling disappointingly thin. Reading reviews and looking at the blurb I felt that I was promised tension, deduction, and deeper problem-solving. Unfortunately, it never fully delivers on that potential.

The biggest issue is simply its length. Just as the mechanics start to click and the world begins to feel intriguing, the game is over. It ends before it can build momentum or explore its own ideas in any meaningful way. What could have been a gripping investigation feels more like the prologue to a larger game that never arrives.

The story also ends up predictable. Key beats begin to telegraph themselves early, and the ending lands exactly where you expect it to. Without twists, red herrings, or layers to peel back, the narrative lacks the depth needed to keep you engaged or surprised.

The investigations themselves feel shallow as well. Each case presents a problem, but they’re often solved with just a few simple steps. There’s rarely a need to dig deeper, only once or twice was I cross-referencing clues, or genuinely thinking like an investigator. Instead of complex puzzles or branching deductions, you get straightforward tasks that resolve too quickly to be satisfying.

Overall, The Operator is an interesting idea wrapped in a very short, very predictable package. If you’re looking for a brief atmospheric diversion, it works—but if you want a substantial investigative experience, this one doesn’t reach far enough.

Okay, while I said I liked this game, [b]I think in terms of recommendation, this is more a "maybe" than an outright "yes."[/b] There are several things to consider before you purchase this one, and while I ultimately think you'll enjoy the experience either way, you may be slightly frustrated by at least one or two of these points. I know I was. 

(-) First, the game is short. It took me less than 4 hours to finish it, and that's with several long cut scenes. Speaking of those cut scenes... pay attention to them. I didn't, because some of them seemed pointless, and that led me to the only time I felt truly stuck in this game LOL.

(+) You play as an operator in the FDI, and the entire gameplay involves sitting in front of your computer, connecting dots, and solving puzzles. I absolutely loved it. It was fresh and interesting, and the feeling of things connecting and unraveling was really fun. I actually wish we had more of it—I would've gladly played more hours of more cases, slowly connecting them to this huge conspiracy. It made me hope that someone would make an entire mystery murder game (as opposed to a conspiracy) as "the guy in the chair," slowly unraveling everything and helping the "heroes" solve the mystery. 

(-/+) For a game that's sitting in front of your computer... the stakes are high and so is the tension. I actually got really anxious at parts, in a way that doesn't really happen with most games because, the way everything is set up, WE are Tenner. So I felt like there was a gun aimed at [i]me[/i] at times, LOL. For me, this was a point in favor of the game, but if you're looking for a more relaxed experience, this may not be it. 

(-/+) The ending. Personally? Not a fan. Oh, I loved the reveal. The minute [i]I[/i] started connecting the dots, my stomach dropped. 10/10 for that. But everything after that?... I will be playing the next game, if there is one, but overall, [spoiler]I am not really the kind of person to enjoy an "everybody died" ending. After all the brilliant puzzle solving, I wanted these characters to have a good ending. I have seen people talk about how this was actually a good ending - how Hal is still thwarting the organization 30 years later, and that's realistic and optimistic but damn. I got attached to [i]these[/i] characters. I wanted to see them happy, even if we fail to totally crush the bad guys in the end of the game. And I wanted to understand what the goal of the "bad guys" in this game is, and I don't. They're evil people, but... why are they doing what they're doing? No clue. Which is another thing I don't like. For me, a game needs to be able to stand on its own, even if it's part of a larger narrative. [/spoiler] Essentially, this felt like a game meant to [i]set up[/i] another game, and truthfully, I don't like that.

review_text_raw:
Aesthetically pleasing, good story with at the very least, decent voice acting if not great. Runs well. An interesting gameplay mechanic that has you sitting at your desk, putting together pieces of the puzzles as agents sweep the field for evidence and follow the leads you help develop. The story has you unraveling a conspiracy, using computer tools, metadata, and analyzing software to pull the narrative together. It's fascinating, and the game does a really good job at making you feel like you're truly a professional analyst, solving crimes from the comfort of a desk in Washington DC.

Problem is, the game is pretty darn short. Only about 4 hours of gameplay, and it feels deeply on rails, to the point that the puzzle portion of it feels more like a addon to the rest of the game. If you subscribe to the $1 per hour mindset, even discounted to $9, this game is technically not worth it, as the game has limited replayability. Though, the game does make up for it with the story and gameplay to a degree. It is, at the very least, a pretty impactful 4 hours, and you could get somewhat different results if you repeat the story, so there is a small sense that your choices matter. 

I might just be spoiled, coming off of The Roottrees are Dead which had a fairly similar premise of using a computer to uncover information that can fill in the blanks. But in TRaD, they introduce you to the tools and then you spend a bulk of the time using them on your own to fill in profiles on the family tree. There was a lot more blanks to fill in and time to spend fiddling around with information. With TO, you get introduced to cool mechanics and tools on your computer, and then use almost none of them ever again. The game feels like a 4 hour tutorial other than the story, which takes interesting turns and, as a flipside, keeps the player continously faced with new and interesting problems to solve. It sucks not being able to repeatedly use a mechanic I got familiar with or a handbook I just learned, but every in-game day pulls me straight in with a curveball, gameplay wise or story wise.

The ending kinda left a bad taste in my mouth. AFAIK, your choices don't really seem to affect the ending from what I saw online in guides and gameplay.

Still gonna leave it as a positive review, because I quite enjoyed this and I think the devs are absolutely cooking here. I just hope the developers consider putting more meat on the bones of TO2, because it feels like there is a ton of potential for a truly great puzzle/detective game here that only gets partially realized.

review_text_raw:
This is an excellent, short puzzle and story game as an Operator in the FDI assisting agents with cases

The game opens with a cut scene which you watch and this sets the tone. Then you see a computer terminal boot up and you log in. This is the start of your job as an operator for the FDI (Federal Department of Intelligence). This is the main screen you see and involves taking calls, running through evidence and assisting agents with their cases.

There is a small cast of characters – you assist a few agents, you hear from the director, who is a friend, and you have a direct supervisor. There are also a couple of other people you hear from. To start with the calls walk you through the basics of the set up and the mechanics you will be using. Then you are given your first call from an agent.

The element of “assisting” agents is fun and about solving puzzles. Finding people in databases, working out how to get evidence from clues in video and audio files and some careful reading of instructions and asking questions. I found the puzzles varied, fun, hard (but not too hard) and appropriate to the setting. The difficulty curve generally increases as the game progresses.

The other people are interesting and I generally liked them, particularly the agents. They were varied, plausible and interesting. There were a couple of dialogue choices where I would have not chosen from the options given, but mostly they were plausible too.

The progression of the different cases builds the stories, tone and difficulty of the puzzles. Also, the puzzles generally get harder, although one or two of the later ones are still quite quick. 

Video and audio are basic but effective, this isn't a high budget game but makes excellent use of what it has.

Saving happens when you exit the game, this isn't particularly clear to start with. I think the rule is that if you are between cases then you just save, but if you are in the middle of a call, then it will take you back to the start of the call/case. Which has the advantage of letting you return to the game and not be in the middle of something complicated, it is also something you can use if you want another attempt at a puzzle (as you can fail some of them).

I won't say too much about the ending. There is only one ending (confirmed by the game designer) and it does seem a little sequel-hook like. Also, there is a post credits scene.

In general, this is a really interesting puzzle story game and be aware of it's comparatively short length.

When I played the demo for The Operator, I knew I was onto something special. I gave it a spin on release day and liked it so much I did a second run-through to pick up all the pieces I missed and see the alternate paths I didn't take the first time.

The Operator's premise is simple; you're an operator for the FDI who handles agent's queries. An agent on the ground will send you photos and videos of what they're seeing, and you have to find the information the agent wants. This includes finding the data or the discrepancy and clicking on it, Papers Please style. And your first day doesn't even finish before something seriously odd starts happening.

The Operator comes in at 3-4 hours of playtime, with an extra hour or two if you decide to replay for all the tidbits like I did. At its price point, some people may dislike that it doesn't hold up to the golden ratio of "one dollar for one hour of game time." Fortunately, this game proves the positive side of the adage "you get what you pay for," because it's by no means an ordinary game.

From the excellent story, to the gripping twists, to the fully voiced characters and the brain-melting puzzles, The Operator is well worth the asking price. My absolute favourite part of the game is its sound design; there are musical stings when evidence appears, and little ramp-ups when a case progresses. My fave parts in the game happened because the game detected that I'm on the right track with solving a puzzle and ramped up the music in response. It gives an incredible cinematic feel that makes you feel like you're in a movie.

I understand that most people will probably feel uneasy paying what the developer asks to get 3-4 hours of gameplay, and if that's you, I recommend wishlisting and coming back when it's on sale. But if you can bite the bullet, you'll find that the game will be more than happy to make every last cent worthwhile.

[b]IF YOU LIKE THIS, TRY:[/b] Home Safety Hotline
This game shares a similar length, premise, and price of another fave of mine; Home Safety Hotline. While The Operator builds on suspense, thrill, and high-stake moments, Home Safety Hotline is surreal, fantastical, and even a little but humorous. As such, if The Operator leaves you wanting more, I recommend this one, too.

Unfortunate to release a game like this in-between the Golden Idol game, as it makes look like it could a smilar type of investigation game. This is not really the case, even though you could really batch it with it and Obra Dinn as point & click made for people prejudicied against point & click, The Operator have more stronger emphasis on its narrative over the actual case solving.

This probably no biggest departure between what you could expect compared to what the game delivers so it's probably what needs to be the clearest : this isn't some X-files case solving about solving stranges cases and chasing aliens, this is short narrative game. While I kinda wish it had more filler cases, that would require to use all the different tools to solve, it's clearly outside the scope of this game. The story itself is a very typical thriller, to the point is possible to get where it's trying to go just because the trope used are that common and maybe it would a problem if this was a visual novel.

The obvious gimmick here is the entire game is told through the screen of a computer, a very limited dispositive that get the most out of the very conventional plot. This may sound dismissive thriller are very codified type of story, that's part of the interest in even saying "this is a thriller", the same way I expect to see a group of young people sharing their sob stories and their way to save the world in my J-RPG. So how do you make something like this interesting when you can't hire Keanu Reeves to do cool stuff on screen ? What the Operator does is giving as little as possible. Low quality camera footage, damaged photography, unreliable testimony, chat windows and a lot of phone calls, an quick acces to a lot clues but very little interaction with the actual narrative. Backed-up by the dynamic soundtrack, this game creates some pretty sincere moment of tension. Especially when the main character position matches the player playing the game, good for immersion even if you don't emphasize too much with the character (I didn't really, sorry).

I do think this game overall is a bit short and lack a bit of substance as an investigation game, but is a narrative game really dedicated to its theme.

While I kinda wish it had more filler cases, that would require to use all the different tools to solve, it's clearly outside the scope of this game. The story itself is a very typical thriller, to the point is possible to get where it's trying to go just because the trope used are that common and maybe it would a problem if this was a visual novel. The obvious gimmick here is the entire game is told through the screen of a computer, a very limited dispositive that get the most out of the very conventional plot. This may sound dismissive thriller are very codified type of story, that's part of the interest in even saying "this is a thriller", the same way I expect to see a group of young people sharing their sob stories and their way to save the world in my J-RPG. So how do you make something like this interesting when you can't hire Keanu Reeves to do cool stuff on screen ? What the Operator does is giving as little as possible. Low quality camera footage, damaged photography, unreliable testimony, chat windows and a lot of phone calls, an quick acces to a lot clues but very little interaction with the actual narrative. Backed-up by the dynamic soundtrack, this game creates some pretty sincere moment of tension. Especially when the main character position matches the player playing the game, good for immersion even if you don't emphasize too much with the character (I didn't really, sorry). I do think this game overall is a bit short and lack a bit of substance as an investigation game, but is a narrative game really dedicated to its theme.

review_text_raw:
I did enjoy The Operator, but it's very much one of those titles I wish I could give a sideways thumb to. I can't explain why without spoilers, so I'll tag that section.

This is one of those games that takes place entirely in menus, but still manages to have a compelling story with some puzzling that keeps you engaged in relatively simple game play systems by making you use the analytical parts of your brain. Taking place in a fictional early 1990s where people have cell phones and wireless Internet access, you're playing as a remote operator at the Not FBI who is tasked with helping field agents analyze data relevant to their cases. As you progress, you'll start to become embroiled in a huge conspiracy that goes through many elements of the agency and other places as well. The interface is nice, the music is good and the voice acting of the characters is actually great. If you like stuff that's more action focused, this might not be for you, but I was kept engaged throughout.

Non-specific spoilers and attached criticisms below:

[spoiler]Unfortunately, this game is really let down by it's in my opinion, pretty awful ending. Things come to a head very quickly and the conclusion is thrown at you over just a couple of minutes and isn't well paced. Things somehow manage to end on both a massive cliffhanger, but also very definitively, making the story unsatisfying and also not necessarily possible to continue in a sequel or expansion. You're introduced to some pretty cool investigative mechanics early on that only ever get used once and you also make many what seem like important choices, but you're given a very strong indication by the end that none of them ultimately mattered, nor impacted the outcome. People have said in the forums that there's little narrative value to additional playthroughs.

As a result, the story goes from intriguing and tense to being a big let down and feels like it was rushed and not fully planned out. This took an otherwise great experience and knocked a lot of wind out of its sails for me.

I still recommend this, but definitely on sale. I'm hoping that the developer puts out some content updates to expand the ending more, but I'm not expecting that.[/spoiler]

review_text_raw:
[h1]The Operator – Review[/h1]
I’ve just finished my first playthrough of [i]The Operator[/i], and it really got under my skin. At first, it feels like a clear throwback to [i]Orwell[/i] — digging through files, connecting clues, and sitting with that constant, uneasy sense of surveillance. The retro desktop setup is spot-on and makes the whole thing feel strangely real. About halfway through, I started wondering if the game itself was testing me. Was I part of the experiment? That thought stuck with me right to the end. The puzzles are clever and rewarding, and the story ramps up quickly, leaving you with plenty to think about. I’m already planning another run to see what I missed.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]What Holds It Back[/h2]
That said, the biggest drawback is its length. At around three to four hours, it ends just as you’re fully immersed. I couldn’t help but think how much more replayable it could be with a few extra systems layered on top.
[list]
[*]Randomised agents
[*]Modular or shuffled case fragments
[*]Overlapping investigative threads across multiple cases
[/list]
Something like that would fit perfectly with the game’s investigative tone and make it feel less like a one-and-done experience. Piecing together evidence that changes each run would add a lot of longevity.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Similar Games Worth Mentioning[/h2]
If you enjoyed [i]Orwell[/i] or [i]Her Story[/i], you’ll feel right at home here. That said, if you’re looking for longer playtime, there are other options worth considering:
[list]
[*][b]Orwell[/b] – branching choices across multiple episodes
[*][b]Return of the Obra Dinn[/b] – a sprawling mystery with dozens of characters
[*][b]The Case of the Golden Idol[/b] – interconnected cases with deep logic puzzles
[*][b]Cyber Manhunt[/b] – hacking and social engineering-driven investigations
[*][b]Shadows of Doubt[/b] – a procedural detective sandbox with near-infinite replayability
[/list]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]
This is a short, sharp, and stylish thriller that absolutely nails its atmosphere and narrative hooks. It’s not perfect — some dialogue feels stiff, and the illusion of choice can occasionally be frustrating — but for a few hours of tense, thought‑provoking gameplay, it’s absolutely worth it. I just hope a possible sequel takes the next step and gives us the freedom to dig deeper, for longer.

[b]Recommendation:[/b] [u]Recommended[/u]

review_text_raw: This game was very positively reviewed. However, I found it to be very disappointing. The term 'game' might not apply, it was really just multi-media fiction with Simon Says style 'puzzles' "Simon didn't say cut the green wire!" The game scolds you for making a single mistake, literally your Supervisor in the game calls you and scolds you. The cut scenes are weird blurry messes with some background noise, but you can't skip, because it turns out there are clues in those that you need for later 'puzzles'. Thankfully they are about as subtle as a brick thrown through the window. I usually like these sorts of games, but this one was very disappointing.
